questions.question: Which of the following statements about threads is/are TRUE?

options.A: Threads can only be implemented in kernel space
options.B: Each thread has its own file descriptor table for open files
options.C: All the threads belonging to a process share a common stack
options.D: Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Threads can also be implemented in user space (user-level threads) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- The file descriptor table belongs to the process and is shared by all its threads [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Every thread has its own stack (and registers, PC) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Threads share the same address space, so one thread can read/overwrite another thread's data; there is no protection between them [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

questions.question: Which of the following process state transitions is/are NOT possible?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Ready: possible (preemption / time slice over).
- Waiting [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Running: NOT possible. When the I/O finishes, the process goes to Ready; only the scheduler can move it to Running.
- Ready [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Waiting: NOT possible. A process can block (request I/O) only while it is running.
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Terminated: possible (exit).

Answer: Waiting to Running, Ready to Waiting

questions.question: Consider a demand paging memory management system with 32-bit logical address, 20-bit physical address, and page size of 2048 bytes. Assuming that the memory is byte addressable, what is the maximum number of entries in the page table?
questions.explanation:
Page size [latex]=2048=2^{11}[/latex] bytes, so the page offset field needs [latex]11[/latex] bits.

With a [latex]32[/latex]-bit logical address, the remaining bits form the page number: [latex]32-11=21[/latex] bits.

The page table needs one entry per possible page number, so the maximum number of entries [latex]=2^{21}[/latex].

Answer: [latex]2^{21}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a paging hardware with a TLB. Assume that the entire page table and all the pages are in the physical memory. - TLB miss: 10 + 80 (page table) + 80 (data) = 170

EMAT = 0.6 [latex]\times[/latex] 90 + 0.4 [latex]\times[/latex] 170 = 54 + 68 = 122

Answer: 122

questions.question:
Recall that Belady's anomaly is that the pages-fault rate may increase as the number of allocated frames increases. Now consider the following statements:

S1: Random page replacement algorithm (where a page chosen at random is replaced) suffers from Belady's anomaly
S2: LRU page replacement algorithm suffers from Belady's anomaly

Which of the following is CORRECT ?

options.A: S1 is true, S2 is true
options.B: S1 is true, S2 is false
options.C: S1 is false , S2 is true
options.D: S1 is false, S2 is false

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Random replacement can evict an unlucky page in the bigger memory, so faults can increase with more frames [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S1 TRUE.
- LRU is a stack algorithm (the pages in k frames are always a subset of those in k + 1 frames), so no Belady anomaly [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S2 FALSE.

Answer: S1 is true, S2 is false

questions.question:
A shared variable x, initialized to zero, is operated on by four concurrent processes W, X, Y, Z as
follows. Each of the processes W and X reads x from memory, increments by one, stores it to
memory, and then terminates. Each of the processes Y and Z reads x from memory, decrements by
two, stores it to memory, and then terminates. Each process before reading x invokes the P
operation (i.e., wait) on a counting semaphore S and invokes the V operation (i.e., signal) on the
semaphore S after storing x to memory. Semaphore S is initialized to two. What is the maximum
possible value of x after all processes complete execution?
questions.explanation:
S = 2 lets two processes be inside at once. To maximise x, make the decrements get lost:

- W reads x = 0 (and holds).
- Y runs fully: x = [latex]-[/latex]2; then Z runs fully: x = [latex]-[/latex]4.
- W stores 0 + 1 = 1 (overwriting [latex]-[/latex]4).
- X runs: x = 2.

Answer: 2

questions.question:
Consider a 32-bit system with [latex]4 \mathrm{~KB} [/latex] page size and page table entries of size 4 bytes each. Assume [latex] 1 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{10} [/latex] bytes. The OS uses a 2-level page table for memory management, with the page table containing an outer page directory and an inner page table. The OS allocates a page for the outer page directory upon process creation. The OS uses demand paging when allocating memory for the inner page table, i.e., a page of the inner page table is allocated only if it contains at least one valid page table entry.
An active process in this system accesses 2000 unique pages during its execution, and none of the pages are swapped out to disk. After it completes the page accesses, let [latex] X [/latex] denote the minimum and [latex] Y [/latex] denote the maximum number of pages across the two levels of the page table of the process.
The value of [latex] X+Y [/latex] is _____
questions.explanation:
Page size [latex]2^{12}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 20-bit page number. One page holds [latex]2^{12}/4=1024[/latex] entries, so 10 bits outer + 10 bits inner; each inner page-table page covers 1024 pages.

Minimum (X): the 2000 pages are contiguous [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\lceil2000/1024\rceil=2[/latex] inner pages + 1 outer page = 3.
Maximum (Y): each page falls in a different inner table, but there are only 1024 outer entries [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1024 inner pages + 1 outer = 1025.

[latex]X+Y=3+1025=1028[/latex]

Answer: 1028

questions.question:
[latex]P = \{P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\} [/latex] consists of all active processes in an operating system. [latex]R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\} [/latex] consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system.
The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.

[latex] \text{Assignment edges: } R_1 \to P_1, R_2 \to P_2, R_3 \to P_3, R_4 \to P_4 [/latex] (the assignment edge [latex]R_1 \to P_1[/latex] means resource [latex]R_1[/latex] is assigned to process [latex]P_1[/latex], and so on for others)

[latex] \text{Claim edges: } P_1 \to R_2, P_2 \to R_3, P_3 \to R_1, P_2 \to R_4, P_4 \to R_2 [/latex] (the claim edge [latex]P_1 \to R_2[/latex] means process [latex]P_1[/latex] is waiting for resource [latex]R_2[/latex], and so on for others)

Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?

options.A: Aborting [latex]P_1 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
options.B: Aborting [latex]P_3 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
options.C: Aborting [latex]P_2 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
options.D: Aborting [latex]P_1 [/latex] and [latex]P_4 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.

questions.explanation:
Build the resource-allocation graph and look for cycles (with single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock):

Cycle A: [latex]P_1\to R_2\to P_2\to R_3\to P_3\to R_1\to P_1[/latex] (involving [latex]P_1,P_2,P_3[/latex]).
Cycle B: [latex]P_2\to R_4\to P_4\to R_2\to P_2[/latex] (involving [latex]P_2,P_4[/latex]).

Both cycles share [latex]P_2[/latex] as a common process. Aborting [latex]P_2[/latex] alone breaks both cycles simultaneously (removing [latex]P_2[/latex]'s edges collapses both cycles at once) — system becomes deadlock-free.

Aborting [latex]P_1[/latex] alone only breaks Cycle A; Cycle B (which never involved [latex]P_1[/latex]) remains fully intact — still deadlocked. Similarly, aborting [latex]P_3[/latex] alone only touches Cycle A, leaving Cycle B untouched — still deadlocked.

Aborting both [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] together: removing [latex]P_1[/latex] frees [latex]R_1[/latex] (letting [latex]P_3[/latex]'s wait resolve), and removing [latex]P_4[/latex] frees [latex]R_4[/latex] (letting [latex]P_2[/latex]'s wait for [latex]R_4[/latex] resolve); with both freed, the remaining chain ([latex]P_2,P_3[/latex]) can fully unwind — deadlock-free.

Answer: Aborting P2 alone works; and aborting both P1 and P4 together works.

questions.question:
Consider a storage disk with 4 platters (numbered as 0, 1, 2 and 3), 200 cylinders (numbered as 0, 1, ... , 199), and 256 sectors per track (numbered as 0, 1, ... , 255). The following 6 disk requests of the form [sector number, cylinder number, platter number] are received by the disk controller at the same time:

[120, 72, 2] , [180, 134, 1] , [60, 20, 0] , [212, 86, 3] , [56, 116, 2] , [118, 16, 1]

Currently the head is positioned at sector number 100 of cylinder 80, and is moving towards higher cylinder numbers. The average power dissipation in moving the head over 100 cylinders is 20 milliwatts and for reversing the direction of the head movement once is 15 milliwatts. Power dissipation associated with rotational latency and switching of head between different platters is negligible.

The total power consumption in milliwatts to satisfy all of the above disk requests using the Shortest Seek Time First disk scheduling algorithm is _______.
questions.explanation:
Only cylinders matter. SSTF from 80: 86 (6), 72 (14, reverse), 116 (44, reverse), 134 (18), 20 (114, reverse), 16 (4).

Movement = 200 cylinders [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 20 = 40 mW. Reversals = 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 15 = 45 mW.
Total = 85 mW

Answer: 85
